title: Shankara in the king's body
hookLine: Shankara leaves his body in a cave and lives as a king, and behind the story sits an old teaching: you are not your body, or even your mind
carry: you wear the body; you are the seer
last: THE BOATMAN'S PENNY — POWERS AREN'T THE GOAL.

cards: Tradition tells a story about the great teacher Shankara. He has just won a well-known debate against the scholar Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife, the brilliant Ubhaya Bharati, takes up the challenge herself.
She asks him about love between husband and wife. Shankara, a lifelong monk, has no answer. So he asks for time.
He leaves his own body in a cave, guarded by his students, and enters the body of a king who has just died. He lives as that king for a while, learns what he needs, and comes back.
Today's sutras name that very power, and others just as startling.

teach.b: Sutra 3.38: by loosening what binds the mind to one body, and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another body. Para-sharira-avesha. More follow.
3.39: master udana, the upward breath, and the body rises. 3.40: master samana, the breath at the center, and a radiance. The classical commentators read these as real.
They can, because of what Hindu thought says a person is.
In the Samkhya-Yoga picture, the body is made of nature, prakriti. So is the mind, just far subtler. That's how a mind might move from one body to another, the way Shankara did.
You are the seer, purusha, the one who watches body and mind. The Upanishads call it atman, the self.

And the Gita gives the picture every Hindu child hears: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new. That's what Hindus mean by rebirth.

teach.h: YOU WEAR THE BODY; YOU ARE THE SEER.
teach.b: It's also why, at a Hindu funeral, many families say the one who wore the body has gone on. Shankara, in the story, didn't stay a king. He learned what he came for, and went back to his own body and his work.
Today that's worth remembering on the days the body feels like everything: a mirror, an illness, an age. You wear it, and it matters. It isn't the whole of you.

how: Hindus widely teach that the self (atman) is not the body, a teaching voiced in the Bhagavad Gita and behind belief in rebirth; the classical commentaries on the Yoga Sutras treat these powers as real within the Samkhya-Yoga view, and the traditional life of Shankara tells of one used briefly and set aside.

o: a vivid dream of living someone else's life
entering another's body, a power of mastery
a restless spirit taking over a person

games.q: body, mind and seer — tap the pairs.

s: in Samkhya-Yoga, the mind is part of nature like the body
both are prakriti; the mind is subtler. only the seer stands outside.
the Gita compares the body to clothes the self changes
worn-out clothes thrown off, new ones put on.
in the story, Shankara stays a king
he learns what he came for and returns to his own body.

games.q: a hard week with your body: an injury, a mirror day, feeling old. what does Shankara's story offer?
o: you wear the body and care for it, but you are the one who sees it.
the body doesn't matter at all, so ignore it.
your body is all you are, so it's everything.
games.why: Shankara stepped out of his body and came back to it. in Hindu teaching the self, atman, is the seer, not the clothes.

practice: Sit and feel the body: its weight on the seat, the breath moving in and out. Then notice that something is noticing all this. Thoughts come too, and that same something notices them.
Don't try to pin it down. Just rest as the one who watches, a little lighter than the body being watched.

wordCard.voice: Para-sharira-avesha, entering another's body. The first of today's powers, with levitation and radiance, which the classical commentators read as real attainments of mastery.

carryVoice: Your line: you wear the body; you are the seer. Shankara stepped out, and came home. That's day four seventy-four.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 3.38–3.40 (another body; udana and rising; samana and radiance)
Bhagavad Gita 2.22 (the self changes bodies as a person changes worn-out clothes)
Shankara Digvijaya (Shankara enters the body of King Amaruka)
